title: Universally accessible, near-instant cross-border money transfer

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a broadly accessible service that lets people send money across borders and have recipients receive usable funds near instantly, reliably and at low total cost. Its scope includes small payments, geographically diverse currencies, commercially difficult corridors and people who currently face barriers to financial services. Delivering that complete capability would require coordinated payment infrastructure, financial markets and institutions.

An end-to-end transfer must connect the sender’s and recipient’s payment providers, obtain foreign exchange, fund and settle the payment, satisfy applicable legal requirements and provide effective fraud controls and consumer protection. Recipient-provider acceptance and recipient access to funds are separate events. The proposed service would need to deliver funds to the recipient and establish enforceable settlement outcomes across the jurisdictions involved.

significance.text: If this service achieved broad reach, affordability and dependable recipient delivery, ordinary users would gain a broadly usable global transfer capability. The transformative change would include making small payments economical and extending reliable service to corridors that attract limited commercial interest. The Nexus report explains how multilateral interconnection could help smaller countries whose transaction volumes make bilateral links less attractive.

The impact depends on access and pricing throughout the complete service. Nexus explicitly acknowledges that access in each country depends on financial inclusion. Its pricing approach relies on competition, with no overall price cap, leaving actual affordability to be demonstrated. Broad technical connectivity would therefore still require accessible customer services, usable recipient accounts or equivalent arrangements, and competitive all-in prices.

Conditional synthesis. Dependable, inexpensive transfers could make remittances and small international payments easier to use and reduce the time users wait for funds. Wider effects on trade, livelihoods or economic development would depend on adoption, local financial access, business conditions and other factors. Those downstream outcomes require separate empirical evidence. The proposed advance combines infrastructure and institutional coordination, and its eventual achievement remains uncertain.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability is sustained, affordable, near-instant recipient delivery across a broad range of jurisdictions, currencies and user circumstances. Engineering barriers include interoperability between domestic instant-payment systems, consistent payment-status handling, near-continuous operation, cybersecurity, outage recovery and coordination among participating providers. Faster messages or a new ledger would address only some of these requirements.

Foreign-exchange provision and settlement funding create economic constraints on coverage. The July 2024 Nexus design requires at least one foreign-exchange provider capable of connecting each supported currency pair directly. Less-used corridors may lack suitable providers. A broad service must attract and sustain liquidity provision in those corridors while keeping exchange-rate margins and other charges affordable for small transfers.

Institutional barriers include governance agreements, enforceable obligations, legal finality, protection of settlement funds in insolvency, dispute resolution, fraud controls and consumer protection across jurisdictions. The report describes legal frameworks and settlement safeguards, while jurisdiction-specific enforceability remains a further question. It also documents the extensive legal negotiations involved in bilateral links. These requirements support the inference that technical interconnection alone cannot deliver the full capability.

Financial inclusion remains an additional barrier. Connecting existing payment systems gives their eligible users a potential transfer route, while people without access to participating financial services still need a workable way to join and receive funds. Universal accessibility would require resolving these local access constraints alongside cross-border integration.

current_state.text: The supplied review establishes several dated achievements. Domestic instant-payment systems already support payments arriving within seconds, and Singapore and Thailand connected their instant-payment systems in April 2021. These results demonstrate operating components and a cross-border connection within a limited geographical scope.

Project Nexus completed a technical proof of concept in 2022. The March 2023 technical report describes a prototype using test systems, with no real-money payments or real customer accounts. This demonstrated technical interconnection under prototype conditions. Production performance, customer access and live settlement across a broad network remained further steps.

On July 1, 2024, the BIS Innovation Hub published a comprehensive Nexus blueprint for standardizing connections between domestic instant-payment systems, building on the earlier proof of concept. The blueprint supplies an architecture and implementation framework. Its publication establishes progress in system design and coordination, while universal availability, broad production coverage and low prices remain outcomes requiring evidence.

The supplied review had partial access to the underlying evidence. Extraction of the July 2024 PDF ended during page 66, leaving later material uninspected. Some pages of the March 2023 PDF lacked extractable text, and its original pages and figures were uninspected. The publication landing page provides a summary of the work. These limitations constrain how completely the technical reports can be characterized.

The supplied freshness record contains no assessment of subsequent deployment through November 1, 2026. Current worldwide coverage, production availability and whether later developments have closed particular gaps therefore remain unresolved in this record. That evidence gap leaves the documented 2021–2024 achievements intact.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. A convincing production service would span geographically diverse currencies and corridors, including low-income destinations and low-volume routes, with near-continuous availability. Evaluation would include small transfers and people previously excluded from relevant financial services. Before testing, evaluators would specify numerical thresholds for delivery time, coverage, affordability, availability and observation duration. These are proposed evaluation dimensions, with thresholds still to be defined.
completion_criteria.label: Production transfers meet predefined performance thresholds across diverse, underserved corridors

completion_criteria.text: The measurement endpoint should capture the recipient’s access to usable funds. Nexus allows a destination payment provider to accept a payment before crediting the recipient, so an acceptance message alone leaves recipient delivery unverified. Evaluation should also examine settlement safeguards and the enforceability of obligations in each participating jurisdiction.
completion_criteria.label: Delivery verification confirms recipients can access usable funds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed verification. Independent evaluators would measure end-to-end delivery times and their distribution, all-in prices including exchange-rate spreads, success and failure rates, fraud losses, dispute handling, outages and recovery. Results should be reported by corridor, transaction size and relevant user group so that aggregate performance does not conceal expensive routes or access barriers. Repeated observations across providers, operating periods and disruption conditions would test reproducibility and resilience.
completion_criteria.label: Independent evaluations report disaggregated performance, full costs and reproducibility

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary. Demonstrations should disclose supported currencies and jurisdictions, eligibility requirements, transaction limits, exceptions, delivery delays and recovery arrangements. Finite testing can establish breadth within those declared conditions. Claims of universal accessibility would require continued evidence as users, corridors, institutions and operating conditions change.
completion_criteria.label: Service boundaries are disclosed, with continuing evidence for universal accessibility

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. FIN-07, Cash-like privacy and resilience for digital money, has the closest explicit overlap. Privacy and resilience could be incorporated into a cross-border transfer service, while each requires its own design and demonstration. Transfer speed and interoperability do not establish cash-like privacy or the resilience properties envisaged by FIN-07. FIN-06 centers on cross-border reach, recipient delivery, cost and access.

Roster-based synthesis. FIN-05, Scalable financing for creditworthy people and firms without conventional credit histories, shares the goal of extending financial access. FIN-06 concerns moving funds across borders. FIN-05 concerns establishing creditworthiness and supplying financing. Progress in payment access could support participation in financial services, while credit access remains a separate capability.

Roster-based synthesis. FIN-02, Causal forecasting and prevention of systemic financial cascades, and FIN-08, A causal theory linking trading activity to market-wide liquidity crashes, intersect with the resilience and liquidity environment of a global payment network. FIN-06 requires operational settlement funding and foreign-exchange provision. Forecasting systemic cascades and explaining trading-driven liquidity crashes involve broader causal questions that a functioning transfer network would leave open.

unresolved_issues: Worldwide deployment, production coverage and subsequent progress through November 1, 2026 remain unassessed in the supplied freshness record.
Numerical definitions of near-instant delivery, low total cost, broad coverage and near-continuous availability, together with observation duration, remain to be specified.
Jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction legal finality, enforceability and insolvency protection have not been demonstrated by the supplied review.
Sustainable foreign-exchange provision and affordable pricing in low-volume or commercially difficult corridors remain open implementation questions.
Practical access for previously excluded users requires evidence beyond connecting existing payment systems.
The July 2024 extraction truncates during page 66. Some March 2023 pages lack extractable text, and original pages and figures were uninspected.
Effects on trade, livelihoods and economic development require separate empirical evaluation.

brief.title: Fast, affordable money transfers across borders for everyone
possible: You could send money abroad and have the recipient use it almost immediately, reliably and at low total cost. The service would reach across currencies and countries, including places with few transfer options and people who struggle to access financial services.
why: Small international payments would become economical, and people sending money home would spend less time waiting for it to arrive. Smaller countries and less-used routes would gain dependable connections even where providers have little commercial incentive to serve them.

sources.who: BIS Innovation Hub and partner central banks and payment system operators
sources.showed: Project Nexus linked test versions of domestic systems that move money within seconds. The team also developed a shared design for connecting these systems across borders, including rules, governance and a commercial model.
sources.quote:
It has 
been tested through a successful 
technical proof of concept that linked 
test versions of the IPS in the 
Eurosystem, Malaysia and Singapore.
sources.cited_for: Nexus demonstrates technical connections and a design for extending them across countries.
sources.not_established: The prototype did not demonstrate real-money delivery, affordable prices or access across a broad operating network.

sources.who: BIS Innovation Hub and central banks of Hong Kong, Thailand, China and the UAE
sources.showed: Project mBridge ran a pilot in which commercial banks made real payments for corporate customers using digital money issued by central banks. Tailored legal agreements supported the payments.
sources.quote:
The pilot advances multi-CBDC experimentation by settling 
real value directly on the platform and on behalf of corporate customers.
sources.cited_for: The pilot demonstrates real cross-border payments on a shared platform with supporting legal arrangements.
sources.not_established: A corporate banking pilot does not establish broad public access or lasting legal certainty across jurisdictions.

sources.who: Wenxin Du, Catherine Huang and David Scharfstein
sources.showed: The researchers compared total transfer costs across banks, money transfer companies and stablecoins, crypto tokens tied to ordinary currencies. Money transfer companies reduced costs, but prices still varied by currency and payment size.
sources.quote:
We find that fintech MTOs
have significantly compressed the costs of cross-border payments, and demonstrate that
stablecoins are not a panacea for frictions in cross-border payments.
sources.cited_for: Comparisons must include the full cost of exchanging currencies and getting money into recipients’ hands.
sources.not_established: The cost comparison does not demonstrate a universally accessible service with dependable, near-instant delivery.

sources.who: Thomas Nilsson, Regis Bouther, Michiel Van Acoleyen and Lior Cohen
sources.showed: Researchers tracked payments through SWIFT, a bank messaging network. Speeds varied widely by route, and much of the delay occurred at the receiving bank before it credited the customer.
sources.quote:
Generally, payments with end -to-end processing times that exceed 
hours or even days tend to spend more time at the beneficiary leg.
sources.cited_for: Delivery measurements need to follow payments through to the recipient’s account.
sources.not_established: The study covers SWIFT gpi payments and does not measure all transfer services or the sender’s full waiting time.

shown: Singapore and Thailand connected their domestic instant-payment systems, letting participating customers send money across the border using a recipient’s phone number. Nexus went further in shared system design, but its technical demonstration used test accounts and no real money.

Project mBridge demonstrated real payments for corporate customers through participating banks. These achievements establish working pieces of the service, while broad public availability remains to be demonstrated.
missing: A sustained service has yet to demonstrate fast, reliable delivery across diverse routes, including access for people excluded from financial services.
Less-used currency pairs still need dependable funding and currency exchange at prices that keep small transfers affordable.
Binding cross-border protections still need demonstration, including fraud remedies, dispute handling and protection if a provider fails.

milestones.label: Live transfers meet agreed standards across underserved routes
milestones.explanation: A live service would have to meet predefined targets for speed, cost, reach and availability across diverse routes and users. This would establish performance beyond favourable test conditions.

milestones.label: Recipients can use the money, with binding settlement protections
milestones.explanation: Testing would have to confirm usable funds reach recipients and payment obligations are legally binding in each jurisdiction. A provider’s acceptance message alone cannot establish completed delivery.

milestones.label: Independent tests report full costs and repeatable performance
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluations would have to report delivery, costs, failures, fraud and recovery by route, payment size and user group, with repeated tests. This would expose hidden weaknesses and establish resilience.

milestones.label: Service limits are clear and accessibility remains demonstrated
milestones.explanation: The service would have to disclose coverage, eligibility, limits, delays and recovery arrangements, with continuing tests as conditions change. This would keep claims of universal access accountable to actual reach.

uncertain: The thresholds for near-instant delivery, low total cost and dependable availability remain undefined, as does how long performance must hold.
Finite trials can establish broad access within stated conditions; how continuing results should justify universal accessibility remains open.

page.title: Cross-border payments meeting G20 retail and remittance targets
page.definition: Cross-border retail payments and remittances, small person-to-person transfers, meet the G20’s published targets for cost, recipient availability of funds, access and customer information. The G20 tracks remittances separately from other retail payments.

goal.need: A study of approximately 20 million SWIFT gpi payments across 141 jurisdictions found route medians ranging from under five minutes to over two days. In January–March 2025, the global average quoted cost of sending USD 200 in remittances was 6.5%.

figures.caption: Processing times for SWIFT gpi payments in September and October 2020.
figures.note: Approximately 20 million payments. Measurement starts when the originating bank forwards the instruction and ends at recipient credit. Recipient-bank offline hours and the sender’s preceding processing are excluded.

statements.quote: An important objective is to enhance cross-border payments for those corridors and end-users disproportionately affected by cross-border payments inefficiencies
enable instant cross-border payments by connecting multiple domestic instant payment systems (IPS) globally.
statements.context: The stated aim of Project Nexus.

completion.title: Retail payments and remittances meet all G20 cost, speed, access and transparency targets.
completion.criterion: Both segments meet G20 targets. Retail: global mean cost ≤1%, no corridor >3%, and all end-users have an electronic sending or receiving option. Remittances: global mean cost for USD 200 ≤3%, no corridor’s SmaRT cost >5%, and >90% of people wishing to send or receive, including unbanked people, have electronic access. SmaRT averages the three cheapest qualifying services. For both, ≥75% of payments provide usable funds within one hour of initiation, per corridor for remittances; the rest within one business day. Initiation is payer-provider receipt. All providers give both parties itemised total costs, exchange rates and conversion charges; expected delivery time; status tracking; and terms.
completion.set_by: G20 cross-border payments programme; FSB targets table, retail and remittance columns. The combined test is presented in a table.
completion.basis: The G20-endorsed targets jointly address cost, speed, access and customer information. They specify an hour rather than seconds and greater than 90% remittance access rather than universality. FSB monitoring uses service-level and account-ownership proxies, which do not establish every target directly.

milestones.title: Cross-border test payments pass between three domestic instant payment systems.
milestones.criterion: A prototype connects test versions of three domestic instant payment systems and processes cross-border test payments. Nexus demonstrated this in 2022 using the Eurosystem, Malaysia and Singapore systems. No real money or customer data were used. The report does not separately evaluate remittances.
milestones.set_by: BIS Innovation Hub, Nexus proof-of-concept programme, described in the July 2024 report. This programme demonstration concerns retail-system interconnection, without a separate remittance endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: used it to connect the test systems of three established IPS:

milestones.title: A live bilateral payment link delivers funds to recipients within minutes.
milestones.criterion: Customers can transfer real money across one bilateral link, with recipient funds arriving within minutes. MAS and the Bank of Thailand announced the PayNow–PromptPay launch on 29 April 2021, initially with daily system limits of SGD 1,000 or THB 25,000. The announcement does not separate remittances from other personal transfers or report a transaction-level latency sample. This is a regulator announcement, not peer-reviewed evidence.
milestones.set_by: Monetary Authority of Singapore and Bank of Thailand, joint PayNow–PromptPay launch specification; initially personal retail transfers.
milestones.threshold_quote: The transfers will be completed within a matter of minutes

milestones.title: Cross-border transfer costs meet the G20’s 1% retail and 3% remittance global-average limits.
milestones.criterion: Retail global mean cost is ≤1%, with no corridor above 3%. For USD 200 remittances, the global mean is ≤3% and no corridor’s SmaRT average exceeds 5%; SmaRT averages the three cheapest qualifying services. In March 2025, quoted USD 1,000 non-remittance personal transfers averaged 2.6% across a sample of 271 providers and 3,407 country corridors. The FSB’s cost datasets omit some receiver-side charges.
milestones.set_by: FSB, G20 cross-border payments programme; 2022 Implementation Report, sections 2.2.1 and 2.3.1. Retail costs are monitored separately by payment use case.
milestones.threshold_quote: with no corridors with costs higher than 3%

milestones.title: At least 75% of cross-border payments make recipient funds available within one hour.
milestones.criterion: At least 75% of retail payments globally, and remittances in each corridor, make funds accessible within one hour after the payer’s provider receives the order; the remainder do so within one business day. The 2025 one-hour service KPIs were 35.4% for retail in March and 54.4% for USD 200 remittances in January–March. These are service shares, not transaction shares; retail excludes person-to-business services, and both omit services without disclosed speeds.
milestones.set_by: FSB, G20 cross-border payments programme; 2021 Targets Report, Table 1 and its initiation and completion definitions.
milestones.threshold_quote: availability of funds for the recipient within one hour of payment initiation for 75% of payments

milestones.title: All retail end-users and over 90% of intended remittance users have an electronic payment option.
milestones.criterion: Every retail end-user has at least one electronic cross-border sending or receiving option. More than 90% of individuals wishing to send or receive remittances have electronic access, including people without bank accounts. Account ownership, 78.7% of adults aged 15 or over, is the FSB’s 2025 proxy; it does not establish cross-border access or identify remittance demand.
milestones.set_by: FSB, G20 cross-border payments programme; the complete numerical access tests appear in Table 1 of the 2021 Targets Report.

milestones.title: All providers give both parties total costs, expected delivery time, payment tracking and terms.
milestones.criterion: Every provider supplies payers and payees total transaction cost, itemising sending, receiving and intermediary fees, exchange rates and conversion charges; expected delivery time; payment-status tracking; and terms of service. In March 2025, 62.9% of cost-transparent retail services also disclosed speed. In January–March 2025, 99% of USD 200 remittance services disclosed fees and exchange-rate margins. These proxies do not establish all four requirements.
milestones.set_by: FSB, G20 cross-border payments programme; 2022 Implementation Report, common transparency target across the payment segments.
milestones.threshold_quote: the expected time to deliver funds; tracking of payment status; and terms of service.

not_found: No published joint test was found requiring delivery within seconds to every potential retail or remittance user.
An FSB cross-border payments KPI report for 2026 was not located.
The Nexus Global Payments website could not be opened.

results.finding: Nexus built a prototype connecting test versions of 3 instant payment systems.
results.detail: The report calls the proof of concept successful, but the supplied text does not explicitly report that cross-border test payments were processed. It does not separately evaluate remittances.
results.quote:
In 2022, working with the Bank of Italy, 
Central Bank of Malaysia, Monetary 
Authority of Singapore, Banking 
Computer Services (BCS) in Singapore 
and PayNet in Malaysia, the Nexus team 
built a working prototype to connect 
the test versions22 of three established 
instant payment systems of the 
Eurosystem, Malaysia and Singapore.

results.finding: USD-outbound emerging-market remittance corridors, sample size unspecified: costs often ranged from 3% to 6%.
results.detail: The result covers selected high-cost corridors from 2022 Q1 to 2025 Q1. It does not establish the global mean cost or corridor-level SmaRT averages.
results.quote:
Using historical remittance costs collected by the World Bank RPW and the CEX FX
data for the same period between 2022Q1 and 2025Q1, Table 6 shows that in high-cost USD-
outbound emerging-market corridors, RPW all-in remittance costs often range between 300
and 600 basis points

results.finding: Nexus prototype connected 3 test instant payment systems and enabled payments across them.
results.detail: The connected test systems were those of the Eurosystem, Malaysia and Singapore. The release does not separately evaluate remittances.
results.quote: Nexus prototype successfully connected the test IPS of the Eurosystem, Malaysia and Singapore, allowing payments to be sent across the three using only mobile phone numbers.

results.finding: Singapore–Thailand retail and remittance corridor (1 corridor): average transfer fees and FX markup fell below 3%.
results.detail: The result covers one corridor serving both retail and remittance payments. It does not establish the global retail mean or costs in every corridor.
results.quote:
Before the linkage, fees and FX 
markup in cross-border transfers averaged 13% of transaction value but have since dropped to 
less than 3%.

results.finding: Singapore–Thailand PromptPay–PayNow linkage: just over 870,000 transfers in 2024; transfers completed within minutes.
results.detail: The linkage serves retail and remittance payments, but the report does not give a remittance-only count or the share completed within one hour. The result covers one linkage in one corridor, not all remittances in every corridor.
results.quote: transfers made via the linkage are completed within minutes.

results.finding: Singapore–Thailand remittance and retail linkage: just over 870,000 transfers in 2024; number of users not reported.
results.detail: The linkage gives participating bank customers an electronic cross-border transfer option. Transfer volume does not establish the share of people wishing to send or receive remittances who have access, including those without bank accounts.
results.quote:
In 2024, just over 870 ,000 transfers were made on the 
linkage, an increase of 16% from the previous year.

results.finding: Singapore–Thailand remittance and retail linkage: fees displayed to senders; sample size not stated; over 870,000 transfers in 2024.
results.detail: The transfer count is linkage volume, not a transparency sample. The report does not establish disclosure to payees, full itemised costs, expected delivery time, tracking or terms for every provider.
results.quote:
■ Greater transparency: fees and charges are transparently displayed to senders before they 
confirm their transfers.
